subject: General guidelines for building a mesh?

messages.author: b548117c8aed3bfb
messages.subject: General guidelines for building a mesh?
parts:
Hi,
 Can anyone point me to some general guidelines for building a mesh for spatially continous models, such as a linear model with a Matern covariance effect?
I was wondering how the minimum edge size of triangles ('cutoff'), maximum size and buffer around the points will affect inferences about model parameters.
Thanks,
Chris

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General guidelines for building a mesh?
parts:
Hi,
I've just written a prototype "shiny" tool to help answer this very question!
It will soon be part of the package, but I'll put up a temporary link tomorrow.
Brief rules of thumb:
1) for alpha=2 (the default spde models), most parameter estimation bias is gone if max.edge is smaller than a 10th of the correlation range. In practice, one can often let max.edge be a bit larger than that. (Bolin&Lindgren 2015 or 2016 says more about this; I'll get the precise reference...)
2) the domain extension to move he boundary effects away from the domain of interest needs to be about the size of the correlation length.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General guidelines for building a mesh?
parts:
On 23 November 2016 at 12:01, <zhe...@bristol.ac.uk> wrote:
Is it possible to control the mesh size by a user specified function in inla.mesh.2d()? Say, a function describing the distance from the boundary when the sampling points are designed to be dense near the boundary but sparse within.

inla.mesh.create() supports a version of this via the quality.spec parameter, but not inla.mesh.2d().
quality.spec allows the user to specify individual max.edge values for each input point, that are then interpolated to other locations as needed.
It's a bit fiddly to get the desired effect from this, so a perhaps easier alternative is to specify a two-stage mesh build in inla.mesh.2d() where the interior of the domain is the second stage. This is done by having the first boundary include a "some distance from the boundary of the domain" boundary.

Finn

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General guidelines for building a mesh?
parts:
What I do is create the mesh iteratively, and use the previous set of mesh$loc for creating the next mesh.

It should be possible to do this in 10 stages and get most kind of meshes.

An example can be found in the tutorial pdf on 
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0B55S_W3X6C38WS13T1NtTVlvblU
around page 16.

Alternatively: Run code 161... file instead.

This tutorial was made for describing boundaries, and may be relevant to you for additional material.

Haakon

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General guidelines for building a mesh?
parts: On 23 November 2016 at 12:46, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
What I do is create the mesh iteratively, and use the previous set of mesh$loc for creating the next mesh.

Yes, this is precisely what inla.mesh.2d() does, by calling the lower level function inla.mesh.create(), plus attempts at preserving boundary and interior segment information.
The tediousness of preserving all the extra meta-data correctly is one of the reasons inla.mesh.2d() hasn't been expanded to allow arbitrary number of iterations, beyond the current 1 and 2.

Finn

It should be possible to do this in 10 stages and get most kind of meshes.

An example can be found in the tutorial pdf on 
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0B55S_W3X6C38WS13T1NtTVlvblU
around page 16.

Alternatively: Run code 161... file instead.

This tutorial was made for describing boundaries, and may be relevant to you for additional material.

Haakon
